entries.clue: Expected firm book binding (2,4)

blocks.note: Co. = company, firm
a tome is a large book; the container instruction opens it around its middle to take the firm's abbreviation inside

annotation.walkthrough: 'Binding' is what books get, which is why it hides so well as the container instruction — the TOME simply closes around the firm.
annotation.definitionFit: Something 'to come' is anticipated but hasn't happened yet, which is exactly what 'expected' means — a plain synonym.

entries.clue: Small story about taking posh cast on tour … (8)

definitions.note: TROUPERS is plural while 'cast' is a collective singular: the one word names a whole company of performers, so the setter may fairly define the plural with it.

blocks.note: s = small, as on clothing labels
'taking' the U it reads REP-U-ORT
U = upper-class, posh

annotation.walkthrough: 'About' turns the whole assembly — S plus REP-U-ORT — end for end, and the ellipsis just runs the surface on into 2 down.
annotation.definitionFit: Troupers are performers who tour together as a company, so 'cast on tour' describes precisely the group the word names.

entries.clue: … band drink meaning Jersey’s cut? (4,4)

blocks.note: a band of people = a crew
to neck a drink = to down it

annotation.walkthrough: The capital J sends you to the Channel Islands; the jersey in question is the woollen one, and its cut is the neckline.
annotation.definitionFit: A crew neck names the plain round-necked style in which a jersey's collar is cut, so 'Jersey's cut' describes it directly.

entries.clue: Spill double (5)

blocks.note: a spill is a thin strip of wood or paper used to carry a flame from a fire to light something else
your double is your exact counterpart, someone who looks just like you

annotation.walkthrough: Two words, no indicator: nearly always two definitions. 'Spill' meaning a fire-lighting taper is old household vocabulary that crosswords keep alive.
annotation.definitionFit: A spill was an old fire-lighting taper, a sense crosswords keep alive; your 'double' is your exact match — two unrelated meanings, one word.

entries.clue: Risk touring America in August (8)

blocks.note: to risk = to imperil; it 'tours' the A
A = America

annotation.walkthrough: August sits at the end of the clue so its capital letter passes as the month; read it as the adjective — august, majestic, imperial.
annotation.definitionFit: 'August' the adjective means grand and majestic, a sense IMPERIAL shares exactly — regal splendour, not the month sharing its spelling.

entries.clue: Theatre feel bitter about lines girl delivers inaccurately (13)

blocks.note: rep = repertory theatre
to resent is to feel bitter about
a girl can be addressed as Miss; the 'lines' instruction opens that word around REPRESENT, which slots inside it

annotation.walkthrough: 'Lines' is the container word — a lining goes inside — and the theatre surface makes you hear an actor's lines instead. Note that 'about' belongs to 'feel bitter about', not to any reversal.
annotation.definitionFit: To misrepresent is literally to deliver something inaccurately — a transparent synonym once the theatre disguise is stripped away.

entries.clue: Doctor: cure can – having killed cold – end patient suffering (9)

blocks.note: anagram fodder — one letter too many
kill a C (c = cold, as on taps) before mixing
joins the fodder

annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' at the head of a clue is the oldest anagram signal there is, and the surface's grim prescription — suffer to the end — is exactly what the answer means.
annotation.definitionFit: Endurance is the capacity to bear hardship without giving in, exactly what patient, prolonged suffering requires — a direct synonym.

entries.clue: Trainee from Bury on reception, ultimately (6)

blocks.note: to bury = to inter; the capital B plays at the Lancashire town
the last letter of receptioN

annotation.walkthrough: 'On' is positional and only works because this is a down entry: INTER sits on the N in the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: An intern is a trainee gaining supervised work experience, a plain modern synonym with no hidden twist.

entries.clue: Sumptuously drunk, sitting on lavatory, exhausted (6)

blocks.note: a drunk = a lush
LAVATORY 'exhausted' — emptied down to its outer letters

annotation.walkthrough: 'Sitting on' is positional in a down entry — LUSH above LY — and 'exhausted' empties a word the way 'on vacation' does at 22 down.
annotation.definitionFit: Lushly means luxuriantly, in rich abundance — a plain synonym for sumptuously, both adverbs describing lavish excess.

entries.clue: Up first in The Open (5)

blocks.note: up = over, finished — as in 'time's up'
its first letter

annotation.walkthrough: 'The Open' reads as the golf championship, which is the disguise: 'Open' alone is the definition, and 'The' only donates its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Overt means open and unconcealed, done without any attempt at secrecy — a direct synonym, not the golf tournament the surface suggests.

entries.clue: Comes after Poles gathered in fruit (9)

blocks.note: poles = fence posts, not North and South
a date, taken in by the POSTS

annotation.walkthrough: 'Poles' are fence posts, not the North and South, and that misdirection is the whole clue. 'Gathered in' is harvest language, and it points the right way round — the container takes the fruit inside.
annotation.definitionFit: To postdate something is literally to come after it in time, so 'comes after' is a direct, near-etymological synonym for the answer.

entries.clue: Ready before clergyman describes Eden? (5,8)

blocks.note: to ready = to prime
a minister

annotation.walkthrough: Eden is a definition by example — Anthony Eden held the office in the 1950s — and the question mark admits it. The surface wants the other Eden, the paradise a clergyman might describe.
annotation.definitionFit: Eden names the answer only by example — Anthony Eden was one Prime Minister, and the question mark admits this is an instance, not a synonym.

entries.clue: Judy’s husband having job say, to get to the other side … (5,4)

definitions.text: to get to the other side
definitions.note: The definition is by example, not by synonym: 'to get to the other side' is the most famous punch line there is — the answer to 'Why did the chicken cross the road?'

blocks.note: Mr Punch, of Punch and Judy
a line = a job — 'what line are you in?'; 'say' marks it as one example

annotation.walkthrough: Fed hides the oldest joke in the language by never telling it: the definition is simply that joke's punch line, quoted.
annotation.definitionFit: This famously is the punch line to 'why did the chicken cross the road' — the definition quotes that joke's ending directly, not a paraphrase.

entries.clue: … of the country. Largely regret going by rail – without one … (5)

blocks.note: most of RUE (regret)
after losing its I
the instruction: I (one) comes out of RAIL

annotation.walkthrough: Two subtractions in five words: 'largely' keeps most of RUE, and 'one' is the I that leaves RAIL. The ellipses just sew this surface to its neighbours.
annotation.definitionFit: Rural describes anything belonging to the countryside rather than a town, so 'of the country' is a direct, everyday synonym.

entries.clue: … track engineer working close to train shed – it’s extortion (12)

definitions.note: RACKETEERING ends in -ing but it is a plain noun here — the name of the crime, as in 'racketeering charges' — so the noun 'extortion' matches it exactly.

blocks.note: anagram fodder — thirteen letters, one too many
shed the N, the close (last letter) of traiN

annotation.walkthrough: A railway surface built to hide railway-free wordplay: 'shed' is the verb, not the building, and 'close to train' names the N it throws away.
annotation.definitionFit: Racketeering is the organised-crime term for running an extortion racket, so 'extortion' names the crime the word denotes exactly.

entries.clue: Charmed by change of demeanour (9)

blocks.note: anagram fodder — nine letters

annotation.walkthrough: 'Change of demeanour' is such an everyday phrase that the instruction hides in plain sight — the change is literal, letter by letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To be enamoured is to be charmed or captivated by someone or something, a plain everyday synonym pair.

entries.clue: Check warehouse facility using powers to knock out door at the back (8)

blocks.note: about to lose a letter
p = power, twice
the R (back of dooR) that the PP knocks out of STORAGE

annotation.walkthrough: A substitution: the PP evicts the R from STORAGE and squats in its place. 'Check' is the noun — a stoppage in play.
annotation.definitionFit: A stoppage is a check on play or progress — a halt imposed from outside — matching the sporting and everyday senses of 'check'.

entries.clue: Juicy gossip for you – Salvador Dali Tate Modern exhibit finally showing (8)

blocks.clueFragment: gossip for you – Salvador Dali Tate Modern exhibit
blocks.note: the last letters of all eight words in a row

annotation.walkthrough: Eight consecutive final letters is a marathon — most setters stop at four. 'Juicy' means salacious, which is what the gossip surface was priming you for all along.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Juicy' as slang for salacious gossip carries exactly the sense 'prurient' does: an excessive, unhealthy interest in sexual detail.

entries.clue: Revenue man in quiet zone checks in on duty at the earliest opportunity (3,9)

blocks.note: duty = tax; 'on duty' hangs the rest after it
spelled straight into the answer
p = piano, quiet, from sheet music
the P checks in as early as it can: S-P-ECTOR

annotation.walkthrough: 'At the earliest opportunity' does precise work: P could lodge anywhere in SECTOR, and Fed tells you to take the first berth, right after the S.
annotation.definitionFit: A tax inspector is literally the government's revenue man, the official who checks what is owed — a plain descriptive synonym.

entries.clue: Very upset about Mark getting awards (6)

blocks.note: SO (very), 'upset' in this down entry
a mark = a scar; O…S closes 'about' it

annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset' can only mean read-upwards in a down clue, and the capital M on Mark is the disguise — no saint or gospel, just a blemish.
annotation.definitionFit: The Oscars are one famous, specific set of awards — the film industry's own — so 'awards' is the general category the answer belongs to.

entries.clue: Viewer’s complaint leads to Musical Youth’s opening piano number being cancelled (6)

blocks.note: the leads (first letters) of those three words
PIANO with its No. (number) cancelled

annotation.walkthrough: Musical Youth were a real 1980s band, which is what sells the surface. The trick to file away: 'number' is the abbreviation No., and PIANO cancels those two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Myopia is short-sightedness, literally an eye complaint that afflicts a viewer's distance vision — a plain medical synonym.

entries.clue: Rumour is, many Ascot odds must be cut (3-2)

blocks.note: cut the odd letters of iS mAnY aScOt and read what is left

annotation.walkthrough: 'Odds' points at the racecourse, but they are the odd-numbered letters — cut them and the evens spell the answer. Note the fodder starts at 'is': even link-looking words can be letters.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Say-so' can mean an unverified claim taken purely on someone's word — the same unsubstantiated assertion a rumour is.

entries.clue: Cool name – probably number one part in nativity play? (9)

blocks.note: cool = in, fashionable
n = name
the goalkeeper — the player who probably wears shirt number 1

annotation.walkthrough: 'Probably' is fair play: keepers usually wear the number 1 shirt, not always. And the question mark concedes the innkeeper never appears in the gospels — only in school nativity plays.
annotation.definitionFit: The innkeeper is the stock role played in every school nativity, so the definition names the exact part by the play it appears in.

entries.clue: Cross old man in Egypt on vacation – he’s far from home (5)

blocks.note: a cross = an X
pa = father
'on vacation' — vacated, leaving only the outer letters

annotation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' means vacated — emptied — a pun worth keeping: Egypt on holiday loses everything inside. The definition is a little sentence standing for the person it describes.
annotation.definitionFit: An expat is precisely someone living far from their home country, so the description substitutes directly for the answer.

entries.clue: Supplies air to a buccaneer on board ship (9)

blocks.note: the A from the clue — not joinery here
a pirate, going aboard
SS = steamship; 'on board' puts the rest between its letters

annotation.walkthrough: 'On board ship' is a fixed convention: inside the letters SS. To aspirate is to supply air — what the h does in 'hat'.
annotation.definitionFit: To aspirate a sound is literally to supply it with breath, the h-sound in 'hat' — a direct technical synonym for 'supplies air to'.

entries.clue: Worry in audition for stage (5)

blocks.note: to faze is to worry

annotation.walkthrough: FAZE and PHASE are exact sound-twins, and 'in audition' keeps the hearing signal inside the theatre. A phase is a stage — of the moon, of a project, of a teenager.
annotation.definitionFit: A phase is a stage of development — of the moon, a project, a life — a plain synonym once decoupled from the homophone's worry sense.

entries.clue: Day after Laurel and Hardy discovered model (8)

blocks.note: Stan Laurel
d = day, placed after STAN
HARDY dis-covered: its outer letters stripped off

annotation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' read as dis-covered — the covers taken off — is a classic worth banking. The famous duo split unevenly: Laurel gives his first name, Hardy only his middle.
annotation.definitionFit: A standard is a model example others are measured against, so 'model' is a direct synonym for the benchmark sense of the word.

entries.clue: Every now and then say, Tati is in French show (6)

blocks.note: every second letter of sAy TaTi
French for 'is'

annotation.walkthrough: Jacques Tati, the French film-maker, keeps the surface in France — where 'is' translates to EST. His name only lends its alternate letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To attest something is to show or demonstrate its truth formally, a slightly formal synonym for the everyday 'show'.
